Q: Exactly what kind of sorting does Visual Studio apply to lines of text? A:

Your environment and criteria:

  • GitLib is used for source code control + CI/CD, this means GitHub's action is out of the question
  • Source code has no lead-in spaces

Currently the team's standard way is to manually use VS's Sort Lines feature, but human operation is not reliable. Someone could forget to do it before submitting the code.

Here's a convoluted solution which surely works, but the team's operation steps need to change.

  • Suppose the source code in question is called source.txt
  • Copy it to a temporary folder first. We will need this copy later.
  • In VS project, use its Add -> New Item... -> Text Template feature to create a new template file, which base name must be the same as your source file, so it should be named as source.tt
  • Edit the template file content as below:
<#@ template language="C#" #>
<#@ output extension=".txt" #>
<#@ assembly name="System.Core" #>
<#@ import namespace="System.Linq" #>
<#
string source =
"""
foo
bar
and more
""";

foreach (string line in source.Split(new[] { "\r\n" }, StringSplitOptions.None)
                              .OrderBy(x => x))
{
#>
<#= line #>
<#
}
#>
  • Edit the previously backed up version of source.txt file in the temporary folder, copy its content and paste into the raw string literal source in place of our foo / bar / and more lines. So from now on this source variable is actually where your team's original "source code" should keep.
  • Team's operation needs to be changed: From now on do not edit the file source.txt directly. Instead, when a modification is needed, open VS and edit source variable's literal string in this source.tt file instead.

Explanation

  • Whenever a .tt file is modified and saved using Visual Studio, T4 engine automatically executes the code in the template file's <# ... #> block.
  • Outside the <# ... #> block is the template content, T4 engine would normally just copy to the output file, which would have the file name with the same base name as the template file but its file name extension would be the one designated by the <#@ output extension=".txt" #> directive.
    • Since the T4 engine always automatically overwrites the original source file, we need to back it up first in temporary folder to avoid being overwritten during this set up process.
  • Directive <#@ template language="C#" #> chooses the language we use in our code, the alternative is VB.
  • Proper indentation is generally recommended in C# code, such as a foreach loop. However, since we don't want extra spaces in front of the output lines, NEVER add any spaces before <#= line #>.
    • <#= expr #> is how we can write any C# expression and its evaluated result will be written to the exact location in output file. For our example, a simple line expression is enough.
  • The code uses OrderBy() for brevity, which is a LINQ extension method. That's why directives <#@ assembly name="System.Core" #> and <#@ import namespace="System.Linq" #> are needed. Should you wish to change the sorting algorithm, it's doable and up to your discretion and you might need to change to different directives for assembly / namespace.

References

  • Writing a T4 Text Template: (official Microsoft document)

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/modeling/writing-a-t4-text-template?view=visualstudio

How to embed a const char in a const string?

Q: How to import file to Tkinter and run script? A:

You can import a Python file in Tkinter like this:

import your_script_name

Phir us file ka function chalane ke liye:

your_script_name.function_name()

Note: Dono files ek hi folder me honi chahiye.

Q: Is it problematic to not check for memory allocation failure in C++? A:

It depends on the your skill level. Under normal circumstances, you should not be dealing with memory management in your own code; it should be already handled by standard library containers that use dynamically allocated memory. In more advanced scenarios you'd be using smart pointers and single object allocations are handled by std::make_shared, and std::make_unique. 3rd tier skill is about providing an allocator class for standard containers who use std::allocator by default; at this level, you should have deep understanding of the allocation+deallocation logic, and decide whether or not to check for memory exceptions. 4th tier skill set is about implementing new container classes that are not present in the std(e.g prefix trie). At this level, you should manage the behavior of your container class in presence of allocation failure.

Tier 1 & 2 memory problems generally lead to automatic abnormal termination of the program. In tier 1, you should only take care not to dangle references. At tier 2, you should take care not to dereference null smart pointers. Tier 3, and 4 require full attention to details of memory management(among other things).

Q: Missing first month in bar chart using R and Rstudio A:

Don't use scale_x_date with labels and breaks, there are date_labels and date_breaks to set dates labels' formats and breaks. In the code below I will not use them. Since there are only two months, I will coerce to factor instead.

First, define a custom theme, with the colors, rotated x axis labels, etc.

theme_custom_q79974513 <- function(){ 
  theme_bw() %+replace%
    theme(
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = 20, angle = 90, vjust = 0.5),
      # axis.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 15, angle  = 45, vjust = 0.5),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#add8e6"),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#eceff8"),
      panel.border = element_rect(colour = "#bdbdd3", linewidth = 2.5),
      legend.background = element_rect(fill = "#eceff8")
    )
}

Now the plot.
The years and months are created and the data is aggregated in a dplyr pipe, then plotted.

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

myColors <- c("OSHA" = "#CB1006", "Non OSHA" = "#1BE4B9")

my_group %>%
  mutate(
    Month = as.Date(Month),
    Year = format(Month, "%Y"),
    Month = format(Month, "%b") |> factor(levels = month.abb)
  ) %>%
  summarise(Incidents = sum(Incidents), .by = c(Category, Year, Month)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Month, Incidents, fill = Category)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = Incidents, color = Category), 
    position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE, vjust = 0.5), 
    size = 5, 
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = myColors) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("OSHA" = "white", "Non OSHA" = "black")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,15), breaks = seq(0,15,1)) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ Year) +
  theme_custom_q79974513()

Created on 2026-07-05 with reprex v2.1.1

Test data

set.seed(1)
n <- 20L
Incidents <- rep(1, n)
Category <- sample(c("OSHA", "Non OSHA"), n, TRUE) |> factor(levels = c("OSHA", "Non OSHA"))
Month <- sprintf("20%02d-%02d-%02d", 
                 c(rep(26:25, times = c(7, 4)), rep(26:25, times = c(5, 4))),
                 rep(1:2, times = c(11, 9)),
                 c(rep(26:25, times = c(7, 4)), rep(26:25, times = c(5, 4))))
my_group <- data.frame(Incidents, Category, Month)

Q: How to reduce Android APK size in react-native? A:

One thing that also makes a noticeable difference is reviewing which native dependencies are actually required and enabling APK/App Bundle optimizations such as resource shrinking, code shrinking, and ABI splits. Even small demo apps can grow surprisingly large due to bundled libraries.

I ran into a similar situation while working on a bus simulator unlimited project, and removing unused packages along with enabling ProGuard/R8 significantly reduced the final package size. It's worth checking your Gradle configuration and analyzing the APK to identify which files are consuming the most space before trying other optimizations.
https://bussidmodhub.com/
